articles.title: What Is Cloud Computing? The NIST Model, CapEx vs OpEx and the Consumption-Based Model
articles.scope: Defines cloud computing with the NIST SP 800-145 wording: five essential characteristics, three service models, four deployment models. Separates measured service (metering) from billing, and contrasts CapEx ownership with consumption-based OpEx. Shows how each characteristic surfaces in Azure and AWS so the reader can explain cloud value in fundamentals and CCSP/CCSK terms.

articles.title: Benefits of Cloud Services: High Availability, Scalability, Reliability, Predictability, Security, Governance and Manageability
IaaS vs PaaS vs SaaS vs FaaS vs CaaS; Public vs Private vs Hybrid vs Community vs Multicloud
articles.scope: Compares service models by what the provider manages versus the customer, and deployment models by ownership and location, including the NIST community cloud. Maps example services on both clouds to each model and gives use-case selection rules, including when multicloud is an anti-pattern and the security implications of each architecture model.

articles.title: The Shared Responsibility Model Across IaaS, PaaS, SaaS and AI Services
articles.scope: Explains which duties shift to the provider at each service layer and which never shift (data, identities, endpoints, access). Contrasts Microsoft's framing with AWS 'security of' versus 'in' the cloud. Shows where to obtain provider evidence for the provider half: Microsoft Service Trust Portal versus AWS Artifact. Links security/ for control-level detail and security/ai-security for AI-as-a-service responsibilities.

articles.title: Regions, Datacenters, Availability Zones, Region Pairs, Edge, Extended/Local Zones and Sovereign Clouds
articles.scope: Teaches datacenters, regions and availability zones, including per-subscription and per-account logical-to-physical zone mapping. Covers Azure region pairs versus nonpaired regions, edge PoPs, and Azure Extended Zones (access by request, several services in preview) versus AWS Local Zones. Surveys sovereign offerings: Azure Government, Azure operated by 21Vianet, Microsoft Sovereign Cloud (Sovereign Public Cloud, Sovereign Private Cloud, National Partner Clouds), AWS GovCloud (US), AWS European Sovereign Cloud and AWS China Regions. Distinguishes data residency from data sovereignty and gives a region-selection method.

articles.title: Resource Hierarchies and Isolation Boundaries: Tenant, Account/Subscription, Group

Maps Entra tenant, management group, subscription and resource group to AWS Organizations, OU and account, with multi-account access-control strategy. Gives a neutral vocabulary used by the provider governance pages.

articles.title: High Availability vs Fault Tolerance vs Disaster Recovery, Scalability vs Elasticity, and Composite SLAs

Teaches SLA mechanics: service credits, exclusions (preview, Spot, single-instance cases) and composite SLA arithmetic for serial and parallel dependencies. Links architecture/reliability for RTO/RPO and DR patterns, and devops/sre for SLOs and error budgets.

articles.title: Zonal vs Zone-Redundant vs Nonzonal (Regional) Resources, and Multi-Region Deployment Models

Covers synchronous versus asynchronous replication, using LRS, ZRS and GRS/GZRS as durability examples. Ends with active-active versus active-passive multi-region designs and region-pair effects, so the reader can pick a deployment type per component.

terms.definition: A model for enabling ubiquitous, convenient, on-demand network access to a shared pool of configurable computing resources that can be rapidly provisioned and released with minimal management effort or service provider interaction (NIST SP 800-145).

The five traits NIST requires of a cloud service: on-demand self-service, broad network access, resource pooling, rapid elasticity and measured service, where measured service means metering usage, not necessarily billing it.

An architecture in which one provider infrastructure serves many customers, logically isolated from each other, which is what makes resource pooling economical and isolation failures a key cloud risk.
Up-front spending on owned assets such as servers and datacenters, which is capitalized and depreciated over the asset's life.
Ongoing spending on services or consumables that is expensed in the period incurred, the accounting model of pay-as-you-go cloud.
A pricing model in which you pay only for the resources you provision or consume, with no up-front hardware purchase.
A service model in which the provider runs hardware, networking and virtualization while the customer manages the operating system, middleware, runtime, applications and data.
A service model in which the provider also manages the operating system and runtime, so the customer deploys and configures applications and data without managing servers.
A service model in which the provider delivers a complete application and the customer manages only its configuration, users, identities and data.
A serverless compute model that runs individual functions in response to events or requests and bills per execution, such as Azure Functions or AWS Lambda.
A service model in which the provider runs the container runtime or orchestrator so customers deploy container images without managing hosts, such as Azure Container Apps or AWS Fargate.

An operating model in which the provider allocates and scales compute automatically and bills only for actual use, so the customer never provisions servers; FaaS is its best-known form but serverless also covers databases and containers.
A deployment model in which a provider owns and operates shared infrastructure that any customer can consume over the internet.
A deployment model in which cloud capabilities are operated for a single organization, on its premises or hosted, giving it exclusive control of the infrastructure.
A deployment model that connects public cloud with private or on-premises infrastructure so workloads and data can be placed, moved and managed across both.
A NIST deployment model in which infrastructure is shared by several organizations with common concerns, such as a regulated sector, and may be operated by them or a third party.
The deliberate use of services from two or more public cloud providers, either for different workloads or for one workload spanning providers.

The division of security and operational duties between provider and customer that shifts with the service model, while data, identities, endpoints and access always remain the customer's responsibility.

A physical facility housing servers, storage and network equipment with its own power, cooling and security; providers group datacenters into availability zones and regions and don't expose them directly.
A geographic area containing one or more datacenters connected by a low-latency network, which is the primary unit you choose for deploying resources and for data residency.

A Microsoft-defined association of two Azure regions, usually in the same geography, used for sequential platform updates, recovery prioritization and services such as GRS; many newer regions are nonpaired.

terms.definition: A provider site outside the regions, close to users, that terminates connections and caches or accelerates traffic for services such as CDN, global load balancing and DNS.

terms.definition: A cloud environment separated physically or operationally to meet a jurisdiction's legal, residency and control requirements, such as Azure Government, Microsoft Sovereign Cloud, AWS GovCloud (US) or the AWS European Sovereign Cloud.
The requirement or guarantee that data is stored and processed in a specified geographic location, which by itself doesn't determine which jurisdiction's laws can compel access.
The principle that data is subject to the laws and governance of the jurisdiction that controls it, which can extend to provider access and foreign legal demands regardless of where the data sits.
The cloud benefit of foreseeable performance (through autoscaling and load balancing) and foreseeable cost (through tracking, forecasting and pricing tools).
The cloud benefit covering management of the cloud (automatic scaling, monitoring, template deployment) and management in the cloud (portal, CLI, APIs and scripts).
The ability of a system to handle more load by adding resources, either vertically or horizontally.
Adding CPU, memory or disk to an existing instance, which is simple but bounded by the largest size and usually needs a restart.
Adding or removing instances that share the load, which requires a distributable, mostly stateless workload but removes single-instance limits.
The ability to add and release resources quickly as demand rises and falls, so capacity tracks load and idle capacity isn't paid for.
The mechanism that implements elasticity by changing instance counts automatically from metrics, schedules or predictions, such as Azure autoscale or AWS Auto Scaling.

A discount for committing to a specific resource type or family in a region for one or three years; it doesn't reserve capacity, except AWS zonal Reserved Instances, which also reserve capacity in one AZ.

A one- or three-year commitment to an hourly spend on eligible compute in exchange for discounts whose flexibility depends on plan type: Azure savings plan for compute and AWS Compute Savings Plans span sizes and regions, while EC2 Instance Savings Plans are bound to a family and Region.
Deeply discounted access to spare provider capacity that can be reclaimed at short notice (30 seconds on Azure, two minutes on AWS), suiting interruption-tolerant workloads.
Charges for data leaving a provider's network or crossing zones and regions, usually free inbound, which often dominate the cost of chatty or multicloud designs.
A per-subscription or per-account, usually per-region, ceiling on how much of a resource you may provision; soft quotas can be raised on request, hard limits cannot.
Provider-enforced limits on request rates to control-plane or data-plane APIs that return errors such as HTTP 429, which clients handle with retries, backoff and batching.
A key-value metadata label attached to a resource for cost allocation, ownership, automation and policy targeting, which grants no permissions by itself.
A preconfigured, governed multi-account or multi-subscription environment with identity, networking, logging and guardrails already in place, into which workloads are deployed.

An organization-wide rule applied above workloads that either prevents noncompliant actions (preventive, such as deny policies or SCPs) or detects them after the fact (detective, such as audit policies or Config rules).
A service address reachable over the internet, protected by authentication and optional IP or network firewall rules.

A network address for a service inside your own private network, so traffic to it never traverses the public internet; implemented as Azure Private Endpoint or AWS interface and resource VPC endpoints.
A network design in which shared services such as firewalls, gateways and DNS sit in a central hub and workload spokes connect only to the hub, which mediates spoke-to-spoke and on-premises traffic.
A compact way to express an IP range as a base address plus prefix length, such as 10.0.0.0/16, used to plan non-overlapping network and subnet address spaces.
Distributing TCP or UDP flows by IP address and port without inspecting application content, either passing packets through or terminating connections.
Routing HTTP(S) requests by content such as host, path, headers or cookies, with a proxy that terminates TLS and can rewrite traffic or host a WAF.
A distributed network of edge caches that serves content close to users to cut latency and origin load.
Rewriting a private source address and port to a public one for outbound connections, so many private hosts share a few public IPs.
Outbound connection failures that occur when all source ports available for a public IP and destination are in use, which NAT gateways mitigate by allocating ports dynamically across more IPs.
A VM image of a firewall, router, SD-WAN or proxy device deployed in a virtual network and placed in the traffic path with routes or a load balancer.
The path-vector routing protocol that exchanges prefixes between autonomous systems, used by VPN gateways, ExpressRoute, Direct Connect and route servers to learn and advertise routes dynamically.
A lightweight protocol that detects link failures in milliseconds so BGP can fail over far faster than its default hold timers.
Layer 2 point-to-point encryption between directly connected routers, used on ExpressRoute Direct and Direct Connect dedicated ports as an alternative to IPsec over the circuit.
An IPsec/IKE tunnel between a network edge device and a cloud gateway that connects whole networks over the internet.
A VPN that connects individual client devices into a network over OpenVPN, IKEv2 or SSTP tunnels, authenticated by certificate, RADIUS or an identity provider.
A VPN that selects traffic for the tunnel by matching prefix pairs (traffic selectors), usually IKEv1 with one tunnel; on Azure it's available only on the Basic SKU.
A VPN that sends traffic into a virtual tunnel interface according to the routing table, supporting IKEv2, BGP, P2S and active-active designs.
Routing all internet-bound traffic (0.0.0.0/0) through an on-premises network or inspection appliance instead of directly to the internet.
Steering traffic through a sequence of network functions such as a firewall or NVA by setting their addresses as next hops, as used to make peered spokes reach each other through a hub.
A periodic TCP, HTTP or HTTPS check a load balancer or traffic manager uses to decide which backends receive traffic.
DNS extensions that sign zone data so validating resolvers can verify answers are authentic, protecting against spoofing and cache poisoning.
The cross-cloud Linux initialization tool that applies first-boot configuration passed as Azure custom data or EC2 user data.
Microsoft's cloud identity and access management service that authenticates users, groups, devices, applications, workloads and agents and issues tokens for Azure, Microsoft 365 and integrated apps.

terms.definition: A named collection of Azure Policy definitions assigned and reported as one unit, often mapped to a regulatory standard or security benchmark.

terms.definition: The action a policy rule takes on a match, one of addToNetworkGroup, append, audit, auditIfNotExists, deny, denyAction, deployIfNotExists, disabled, manual, modify or mutate, evaluated in a defined order.
terms.equivalent: aws: SCP Deny and Config rule remediation (partial)

terms.definition: An object that excludes a scope from an assignment for a documented waiver or mitigated reason, optionally expiring, while keeping it visible in compliance reporting.
terms.equivalent: aws: Config rule scope exclusions (partial)

terms.definition: A job that applies modify or deployIfNotExists policy effects to existing noncompliant resources using the assignment's managed identity.
terms.equivalent: aws: AWS Config remediation action via Systems Manager Automation (close)

terms.definition: An Azure Policy capability that audits or enforces operating-system settings inside Azure VMs and Arc-enabled servers using configuration packages.
terms.equivalent: aws: Systems Manager State Manager (partial)

terms.definition: Applying subscription or resource-group tags to child resources either in cost data only (Cost Management tag inheritance) or on the resources themselves (Azure Policy modify), since tags don't inherit by default.
terms.equivalent: aws: tag policies plus CloudFormation stack tag propagation (partial)

terms.definition: A CanNotDelete or ReadOnly lock on a subscription, resource group or resource that overrides all users' permissions for control-plane operations and is inherited by child resources.
terms.equivalent: aws: termination protection and stack policies, or an SCP Deny (partial)

terms.definition: A legacy service for packaging role assignments, policy assignments, templates and resource groups into versioned definitions, in phased retirement from July 31, 2026 and retiring January 31, 2027 in favor of template specs and deployment stacks.
terms.equivalent: aws: Service Catalog portfolios or Control Tower blueprints (partial)

terms.definition: Microsoft's reference architecture for a governed multi-subscription estate, made of one platform landing zone plus one workload landing zone per workload, deployable through IaC or portal accelerators.
terms.equivalent: aws: AWS Control Tower landing zone or Landing Zone Accelerator on AWS (close)

terms.definition: The centralized part of an Azure landing zone, normally one per tenant, comprising the management group hierarchy, guardrail policies and shared security, management, identity and connectivity resources.
terms.equivalent: aws: Control Tower foundational OUs with log archive and audit accounts (close)

terms.definition: The set of subscriptions for all environments of one workload, placed under the Internal (Corp), Online or Local management group to inherit platform guardrails.
terms.equivalent: aws: workload accounts in a Control Tower OU (close)

terms.definition: An automated, request-driven process that creates subscriptions already placed in the right management group with baseline networking, RBAC, policy and budgets.
terms.equivalent: aws: Control Tower Account Factory or Account Factory for Terraform (close)

terms.definition: Microsoft's adoption guidance organized into Strategy, Plan, Ready, Adopt, Govern, Secure and Manage, with scenarios for data, AI, AI agents, sovereignty and Azure VMware Solution; its Ready phase produces an Azure landing zone.
aliases: Microsoft Cloud Adoption Framework for Azure
terms.equivalent: aws: AWS Cloud Adoption Framework (close)

terms.definition: A service that delegates subscriptions or resource groups in a customer tenant to users and groups in a managing tenant, so they operate across tenants without guest accounts.
terms.equivalent: aws: cross-account IAM roles and Organizations delegated administrators (partial)

terms.definition: A management-group-scoped ARM object that pools IaaS compute quota across EA, MCA or internal subscriptions for self-service transfers, while deployments still check each subscription's own quota.
terms.equivalent: aws: none (Service Quotas are per account) (none)

terms.definition: A regional, isolated private network in a subscription, defined by address prefixes, whose subnets span all availability zones in the region.
terms.equivalent: aws: Amazon VPC (close; AWS subnets are AZ-scoped, Azure subnets are regional)

terms.definition: An address range within a VNet, with five reserved addresses, that spans every zone in its region and is where NSGs, route tables, NAT gateways, service endpoints and delegations attach.
terms.equivalent: aws: VPC subnet (partial; AZ-scoped on AWS)

terms.definition: A subnet with default outbound access disabled, the default for new VNets created with API versions released after March 31, 2026, so VMs need an explicit egress method.
terms.equivalent: aws: private subnet without a NAT route (close)

terms.definition: Designating a subnet for a specific PaaS service, such as App Service integration or SQL Managed Instance, which then injects resources and applies its own network policies there.
terms.equivalent: aws: none (services inject ENIs into ordinary subnets) (none)

terms.definition: A resource holding a static IPv4 or IPv6 address in the Standard or StandardV2 SKU (Basic retired September 30, 2025), regional or global tier, assigned to NICs, load balancers and gateways.
terms.equivalent: aws: Elastic IP address (close)

terms.definition: A reserved contiguous block of static public IP addresses from which you allocate addresses, giving predictable ranges for partner allowlists.
terms.equivalent: aws: contiguous Amazon-provided IPv4 blocks via VPC IPAM (partial)

terms.definition: A resource that onboards an IP range you own into Azure after ownership validation, so you can create public IP prefixes from it and Microsoft advertises it.
terms.equivalent: aws: Bring your own IP addresses (BYOIP) (close)

terms.definition: A public IP setting that carries internet traffic over Microsoft's backbone to the edge nearest the user (default) or hands it to the internet near the region for lower egress cost.
terms.equivalent: aws: none direct (Global Accelerator is the premium path) (partial)

terms.definition: A stateful, prioritized list of allow and deny rules associated with a subnet or NIC, with default rules that allow intra-VNet traffic and deny unsolicited inbound internet traffic.
terms.equivalent: aws: security group (partial; allow-only, ENI-level) plus network ACL (partial)

terms.definition: A logical label for NICs that NSG rules can use as source or destination, so rules follow workload roles rather than IP addresses.
terms.equivalent: aws: security group referenced as a rule source (close)

terms.definition: A Microsoft-maintained named group of IP prefixes for an Azure service, such as Storage.WestEurope, usable in NSG, firewall and UDR rules.
terms.equivalent: aws: AWS-managed prefix lists (close)

terms.definition: A central service that groups VNets across subscriptions into network groups and deploys connectivity (hub-and-spoke, mesh), security admin rules, routing configurations and IPAM pools.
terms.equivalent: aws: Cloud WAN plus Firewall Manager plus VPC IPAM combined (partial)

terms.definition: A static or Azure Policy-driven dynamic set of VNets or subnets that AVNM configurations target.
terms.equivalent: aws: Cloud WAN segment attachments (partial)

terms.definition: An AVNM rule with Allow, Deny or Always Allow actions that is evaluated before NSGs, letting central teams enforce or guarantee traffic that workload owners can't override.
terms.equivalent: aws: Firewall Manager common security group policies (partial)

terms.definition: A route Azure creates automatically for VNet address space, peerings, gateways, service endpoints and 0.0.0.0/0 to the internet, which UDRs and BGP can override.
terms.equivalent: aws: VPC main route table local route (close)

terms.definition: A custom route in a route table associated with subnets that overrides system routes, for example sending 0.0.0.0/0 to a firewall or NVA.
terms.equivalent: aws: VPC route table route (close)

terms.definition: The merged system, BGP and user-defined routes actually applied to a NIC, shown per interface to diagnose routing.
terms.equivalent: aws: Reachability Analyzer path analysis (partial)

terms.definition: The combined subnet and NIC NSG rules, plus AVNM admin rules, actually applied to a NIC, used to explain allowed and denied traffic.
terms.equivalent: aws: Network Access Analyzer findings (partial)

terms.definition: A managed BGP route reflector in a VNet that exchanges routes with NVAs and programs learned routes into the VNet without manual UDRs.
terms.equivalent: aws: Amazon VPC Route Server (close)

terms.definition: A non-transitive, private backbone connection between two VNets in the same or different regions, subscriptions or tenants; allowlisted subnet peering can limit it to selected subnets.
terms.equivalent: aws: VPC peering (close)

terms.definition: A peering setting that lets spoke VNets use the hub's VPN or ExpressRoute gateway for cross-premises connectivity instead of deploying their own.
terms.equivalent: aws: none for VPC peering (Transit Gateway attachments are the AWS pattern) (none)

terms.definition: A Microsoft-managed hub-and-spoke service whose Standard virtual hubs give transitive any-to-any routing between VNets, branches, users and ExpressRoute; the Basic SKU supports only site-to-site VPN.
terms.equivalent: aws: AWS Transit Gateway per hub (close); AWS Cloud WAN for the managed global WAN (close)

terms.definition: A Microsoft-managed regional VNet inside Virtual WAN that hosts the hub router and gateways, firewall or NVAs.
terms.equivalent: aws: Transit Gateway (close)

terms.definition: A Virtual WAN hub setting that sends internet and/or private traffic through a hub firewall or NVA without hand-built route tables.
terms.equivalent: aws: Transit Gateway route tables to an inspection VPC (partial)

terms.definition: A Virtual WAN hub with Azure Firewall or a supported security partner deployed and managed through Firewall Manager policies.
terms.equivalent: aws: Cloud WAN with Network Firewall service insertion (close)

terms.definition: The capacity increment for hub gateways and routing infrastructure, chosen per gateway type to set aggregate throughput.
terms.equivalent: aws: none (Transit Gateway scales automatically) (none)

terms.definition: A managed gateway in GatewaySubnet that terminates IPsec/IKE site-to-site, VNet-to-VNet and point-to-site tunnels; new gateways should use zone-redundant AZ SKUs as non-AZ SKUs are migrated.
terms.equivalent: aws: Site-to-Site VPN on a virtual private gateway or Transit Gateway (close)

terms.definition: An Azure object representing the on-premises VPN device, with its public IP or FQDN, address prefixes and BGP settings.
terms.equivalent: aws: customer gateway (exact)

terms.definition: A per-connection setting that pins encryption, integrity, DH/PFS groups and SA lifetimes instead of the gateway defaults.
terms.equivalent: aws: VPN tunnel options (close)

terms.definition: A VPN gateway whose two instances each have a public IP and establish tunnels simultaneously, usually with BGP, removing the failover delay of active-standby.
terms.equivalent: aws: two-tunnel Site-to-Site VPN with BGP (close)

terms.definition: Microsoft's P2S client that imports a downloaded profile and supports OpenVPN with Microsoft Entra ID or certificate authentication.
terms.equivalent: aws: AWS-provided Client VPN software (close)

terms.definition: A Windows VPN feature that auto-connects device or user tunnels to a route-based gateway with IKEv2 or SSTP and certificate authentication.
terms.equivalent: aws: none (none)

terms.definition: A Windows Admin Center feature that creates a point-to-site VPN connection from a Windows Server to an Azure VNet.
terms.equivalent: aws: none (none)

terms.definition: A VXLAN-based stretch of an on-premises subnet into Azure that lets migrated VMs keep their IP addresses during migration.
terms.equivalent: aws: none native (VMware HCX L2 extension is the usual analogue) (none)

terms.definition: A private Layer 3 connection from on-premises to Microsoft's network through a provider or ExpressRoute Direct, with redundant BGP sessions, private and Microsoft peering and an SLA, not encrypted by default.
terms.equivalent: aws: AWS Direct Connect (close)

terms.definition: Dual 10 or 100 Gbps ports connecting your routers directly to Microsoft's edge without a provider, supporting MACsec and the full FastPath feature set.
terms.equivalent: aws: Direct Connect dedicated connection (close)

terms.definition: The virtual network gateway that links a VNet to circuits, in ErGw1Az-ErGw3Az or scalable ErGwScale SKUs, with a Microsoft-managed public IP and up to 4 circuits from one peering location.
terms.equivalent: aws: Direct Connect gateway with a virtual private gateway or Transit Gateway (partial)

terms.definition: A feature that sends on-premises traffic straight to VMs, bypassing the gateway, on UltraPerformance, ErGw3Az or ErGwScale with at least 10 scale units; peering, UDR and Private Link support need ExpressRoute Direct.
terms.equivalent: aws: none (Direct Connect has no gateway hop to bypass) (none)

terms.definition: A circuit configuration dual-homed to two distinct peering locations in one city, for higher resiliency at the cost of a standard circuit.
terms.equivalent: aws: Direct Connect maximum resiliency across two locations (partial)

terms.definition: The ExpressRoute routing domain that connects on-premises networks to VNets using private addresses.
terms.equivalent: aws: Direct Connect private or transit virtual interface (close)

terms.definition: The ExpressRoute routing domain that reaches Microsoft public services such as Microsoft 365 and Azure PaaS public endpoints over public prefixes, filtered by route filters.
terms.equivalent: aws: Direct Connect public virtual interface (close)

terms.definition: A resource attached to Microsoft peering that selects which BGP communities (services and regions) Microsoft advertises to you.
terms.equivalent: aws: BGP community tags on a public VIF (partial)

terms.definition: A circuit add-on that extends connectivity to all regions globally and raises route and VNet-link limits, compared with Local (one metro region set) and Standard (one geopolitical area).
terms.equivalent: aws: Direct Connect gateway reaching any Region (partial)

terms.definition: An add-on that links two ExpressRoute circuits so on-premises sites exchange traffic over the Microsoft backbone.
terms.equivalent: aws: Direct Connect SiteLink (close)

terms.definition: The default recursive resolver at 168.63.129.16 that every VNet uses unless custom DNS servers are set; it resolves linked private zones but doesn't validate DNSSEC.
terms.equivalent: aws: Route 53 Resolver (VPC+2 address) (close)

terms.definition: An authoritative internet-facing DNS zone hosted on Azure DNS name servers, with optional DNSSEC signing (ECDSAP256SHA256, RFC 9824 compact denial).
terms.equivalent: aws: Route 53 public hosted zone (close)

terms.definition: A record set that points to an Azure resource such as a public IP, Front Door or Traffic Manager profile and updates automatically, including at the zone apex.
terms.equivalent: aws: Route 53 alias record (exact)

terms.definition: A DNS zone resolvable only from VNets linked to it, optionally with VM autoregistration, and used to resolve private endpoint names in privatelink zones.
terms.equivalent: aws: Route 53 private hosted zone (close)

terms.definition: A managed service with inbound endpoints that on-premises DNS can forward to and outbound endpoints with forwarding rulesets for conditional forwarding out of Azure, replacing DNS forwarder VMs.
terms.equivalent: aws: Route 53 Resolver inbound and outbound endpoints with rules (close)

terms.definition: An Azure DNS resource linked to VNets that allows, alerts on or blocks queries using domain lists, including a Microsoft threat-intelligence feed, and logs DNS traffic.
terms.equivalent: aws: Route 53 Resolver DNS Firewall (close)

terms.definition: The platform technology behind private endpoints and Private Link services that carries traffic to a service privately over the Microsoft backbone.
terms.equivalent: aws: AWS PrivateLink (close)

terms.definition: A NIC with a private IP in your subnet that connects to one specific PaaS resource or Private Link service, reachable from peered and on-premises networks, which requires DNS to resolve the service name to that IP.
terms.equivalent: aws: interface VPC endpoint, or resource VPC endpoint for a single resource (close)

terms.definition: Your own service published behind a Standard internal load balancer so consumers in other VNets or tenants reach it through their own private endpoints.
terms.equivalent: aws: VPC endpoint service (close)

terms.definition: A free subnet setting that sends traffic to a PaaS service over the backbone with the subnet's identity, so the service firewall can allow that subnet while the service keeps its public endpoint.
terms.equivalent: aws: gateway VPC endpoint (partial; S3 and DynamoDB only)

terms.definition: A paid service endpoint variant that tags subnet traffic with a public IP network identifier, which a network security perimeter can authorize for services such as Storage, Key Vault, SQL Database and Cosmos DB.
terms.equivalent: aws: none (none)

terms.definition: A policy on a service endpoint subnet that limits Storage access to specific accounts, preventing exfiltration to other accounts over the endpoint.
terms.equivalent: aws: VPC endpoint policy (close)

terms.definition: A GA logical boundary around supported PaaS resources that, in enforced mode, denies public traffic except intra-perimeter and explicitly allowed flows, with transition mode (formerly learning mode) for discovery.
terms.equivalent: aws: VPC endpoint policies plus resource control policies (partial)

terms.definition: A Layer 4 TCP/UDP pass-through load balancer, public or internal, whose Standard SKU is zone-aware, secure by default and offers outbound rules and a Global tier; Basic retired September 30, 2025.
terms.equivalent: aws: Network Load Balancer (close)

terms.definition: A Load Balancer SKU that transparently chains third-party NVAs into the traffic path of a public load balancer or VM IP using VXLAN tunnels.
terms.equivalent: aws: Gateway Load Balancer (close)

terms.definition: A load balancer rule that forwards a frontend port or port range to a specific backend instance, such as SSH to one VM.
terms.equivalent: aws: none (NLB listeners target groups, not single-instance port maps) (none)

terms.definition: An explicit SNAT configuration on a public Standard load balancer that sets which frontend IPs and how many ports backend instances use for outbound traffic.
terms.equivalent: aws: none (NAT gateways provide egress) (none)

terms.definition: An internal Standard load balancer rule that balances all TCP and UDP ports at once, used to make NVA pairs highly available.
terms.equivalent: aws: Gateway Load Balancer (partial)

terms.definition: A regional reverse proxy in a dedicated subnet that provides L7 routing, TLS termination, rewrites, autoscaling and optional WAF, plus a TCP/TLS proxy on v2; Basic is preview and v1 retired April 28, 2026.
terms.equivalent: aws: Application Load Balancer (close)

terms.definition: A global L7 edge service and CDN in Standard and Premium tiers that routes HTTP(S) to the best origin with caching, TLS offload, rules and WAF, and in Premium Private Link origins; classic retires March 31, 2027.
terms.equivalent: aws: CloudFront with AWS WAF, plus Global Accelerator for anycast (partial)

terms.definition: Microsoft's legacy CDN profile, accepting no new resources, domains or managed certificates since August 15, 2025 and retiring September 30, 2027, with Front Door Standard/Premium as the replacement.
terms.equivalent: aws: Amazon CloudFront (close)

terms.definition: A DNS-based global traffic distributor that answers queries with an endpoint chosen by priority, weighted, performance, geographic, multivalue or subnet routing, and never proxies traffic.
terms.equivalent: aws: Route 53 routing policies with health checks (close)

terms.definition: A managed outbound-only SNAT service on subnets that outranks other egress except UDRs to an NVA or gateway; Standard is zonal, and same-priced StandardV2 is zone-redundant with IPv6, NAT64, 100 Gbps and StandardV2 IPs only.
terms.equivalent: aws: NAT gateway (close; AWS offers zonal and regional modes)

terms.definition: Implicit internet egress through a Microsoft-owned, changeable IP for VMs without an explicit outbound method, not offered in private subnets or to Flexible scale set instances.
terms.equivalent: aws: none (AWS private subnets never have implicit egress) (none)

terms.definition: A managed, stateful, autoscaling network firewall in Basic, Standard and Premium SKUs with DNAT, network and application rules and threat intelligence; Premium adds TLS inspection, IDPS and URL filtering.
terms.equivalent: aws: AWS Network Firewall (close)

terms.definition: A central service that manages firewall policies and secured hubs or hub VNets across regions and subscriptions.
terms.equivalent: aws: AWS Firewall Manager (close)

terms.definition: A top-level resource holding rule collection groups and settings that one or many firewalls use, with parent-child inheritance for central baselines.
terms.equivalent: aws: Network Firewall policy (close)

terms.definition: Layer 7 protection attached to Front Door or Application Gateway that detects or blocks attacks such as SQL injection and XSS with managed, custom and bot rules.
terms.equivalent: aws: AWS WAF (close)

terms.definition: The resource holding WAF mode, managed rule sets, exclusions and custom rules, associated with a Front Door domain or an Application Gateway, listener or path.
terms.equivalent: aws: AWS WAF web ACL (close)

terms.definition: Microsoft's managed WAF rule set, based on OWASP CRS plus Microsoft threat intelligence, with anomaly scoring on Front Door and Application Gateway.
terms.equivalent: aws: AWS Managed Rules core rule set (close)

terms.definition: The open-source generic attack-detection rules for ModSecurity-compatible WAFs, offered in CRS versions on Application Gateway alongside Microsoft's DRS.
A managed WAF rule set that classifies good, bad and unknown bots from Microsoft threat intelligence and applies actions per category.
terms.equivalent: aws: AWS WAF Bot Control (close)

terms.definition: L3/L4 DDoS mitigation for public IPs, free as infrastructure protection and paid as IP Protection (per IP) or Network Protection (per plan, adding rapid response, cost protection and a WAF discount).
terms.equivalent: aws: AWS Shield Standard and Shield Advanced (close)

terms.definition: A managed RDP/SSH broker that reaches VMs over private IPs from the portal or native client, deployed in an AzureBastionSubnet of /26 or larger except for the Developer tier.
terms.equivalent: aws: Systems Manager Session Manager or EC2 Instance Connect Endpoint (partial)

terms.definition: A regional suite of network monitoring and diagnostics, including topology, Connection monitor, IP flow verify, NSG diagnostics, next hop, packet capture, VPN troubleshoot, flow logs and traffic analytics.
terms.equivalent: aws: Reachability Analyzer, Network Access Analyzer and VPC Flow Logs (partial)

terms.definition: A configuration-free view of topology, health, metrics, connectivity tests, traffic and a diagnostic toolkit for all deployed network resources.
terms.equivalent: aws: CloudWatch Network Monitoring and Network Manager (partial)

terms.definition: A Network Watcher feature that continuously tests reachability, latency and packet loss between Azure, on-premises and internet endpoints with alerts.
terms.equivalent: aws: CloudWatch Network Monitor (close)

terms.definition: A Network Watcher check that reports whether a specific 5-tuple to or from a VM is allowed or denied and by which rule.
terms.equivalent: aws: Reachability Analyzer (partial)

terms.definition: Legacy per-NSG IP flow logging that accepts no new creation and retires September 30, 2027, superseded by virtual network flow logs.
terms.equivalent: aws: VPC Flow Logs at ENI level (close)

terms.definition: Network Watcher logging of IP flows at VNet, subnet or NIC scope, including NSG and AVNM admin rule decisions and encryption state, to a Standard storage account in the same region.
terms.equivalent: aws: VPC Flow Logs (close)

terms.definition: Processing of flow logs into Log Analytics with enrichment and visualizations of top talkers, open ports, malicious IPs and cross-region traffic.
terms.equivalent: aws: CloudWatch Contributor Insights or Athena over VPC Flow Logs (partial)

terms.definition: Platform encryption of VM-to-VM traffic within and across peered VNets on supported VM sizes, with policies to allow or drop unencrypted flows.
terms.equivalent: aws: automatic Nitro encryption in transit between supported instances (close)

terms.definition: Single-root I/O virtualization that bypasses the host virtual switch to give VMs lower latency, jitter and CPU use on supported sizes.
terms.equivalent: aws: Elastic Network Adapter (ENA) (close)

terms.definition: An IaaS compute instance with a chosen size, image, managed disks and NICs, for which you manage the guest OS and everything above it.
terms.equivalent: aws: Amazon EC2 instance (close)

terms.definition: The Azure VM SKU that fixes vCPU, memory, temporary storage, disk and network limits, named by family, vCPU count, feature letters and version (for example Standard_D4ds_v5).
terms.equivalent: aws: EC2 instance type (close)

terms.definition: The virtual hardware type of an Azure VM, BIOS-based Gen1 or UEFI-based Gen2, which determines support for Trusted Launch and larger disks.
terms.equivalent: aws: BIOS versus UEFI boot mode on EC2 (close)

terms.definition: A security type for Gen2 VMs with Secure Boot, vTPM and boot integrity monitoring, default for new VMs and scale sets in the portal, CLI and PowerShell, and for IaC and SDKs on Compute API 2025-11-01+ when supported.
terms.equivalent: aws: UEFI Secure Boot with NitroTPM on EC2 (close)

terms.definition: A VM security type running in a hardware TEE (AMD SEV-SNP or Intel TDX) that encrypts memory and isolates the guest from the host and hypervisor, with attestation.
terms.equivalent: aws: EC2 instances with AMD SEV-SNP (partial)

terms.definition: A resource that deploys and manages a group of VMs from a model, with autoscaling, distribution across zones or fault domains, and upgrade and repair policies.
terms.equivalent: aws: EC2 Auto Scaling group (close)

terms.definition: The recommended scale set mode that manages standard Azure VMs, allowing mixed sizes, mixed Spot and on-demand instances and standard VM APIs, with no default outbound access.
terms.equivalent: aws: Auto Scaling group with a mixed instances policy (close)

terms.definition: The older scale set mode that manages identical, scale-set-specific instances through VMSS APIs, still used by workloads such as Service Fabric.
terms.equivalent: aws: Auto Scaling group with one launch template (close)

terms.definition: A logical grouping that spreads VMs across fault domains and update domains within one datacenter for a 99.95% SLA, without protecting against a zone failure.
terms.equivalent: aws: EC2 spread or partition placement group (partial)

terms.definition: A group of hardware sharing power and network switch, such as a rack, across which Azure spreads VMs in availability sets or scale sets.
terms.equivalent: aws: partition in a partition placement group (close)

terms.definition: A logical group of VMs in an availability set that Azure reboots together during planned maintenance, one domain at a time.
terms.equivalent: aws: none (none)

terms.definition: A logical constraint that places VMs physically close together to minimize latency, at the cost of capacity flexibility and zone resilience.
terms.equivalent: aws: EC2 cluster placement group (close)

terms.definition: An Azure-managed block volume in one of five types (Ultra Disk, Premium SSD v2, Premium SSD, Standard SSD, Standard HDD), with LRS or ZRS, snapshots and always-on server-side encryption.
terms.equivalent: aws: Amazon EBS volume (close)

terms.definition: Always-on encryption of managed disk data at rest in storage with platform-managed keys or customer-managed keys via a disk encryption set, optionally double-encrypted.
terms.equivalent: aws: EBS encryption with AWS-managed or customer KMS keys (close)

terms.definition: A resource that links managed disks to a Key Vault or Managed HSM key and the identity used to access it, for customer-managed key encryption.
terms.equivalent: aws: KMS key referenced by EBS (close)

terms.definition: A VM option that encrypts temporary disks, caches and data flowing to storage on the host with platform or customer-managed keys, using no guest CPU, and is the recommended replacement for Azure Disk Encryption.
terms.equivalent: aws: EBS encryption with instance store encrypted by Nitro (partial)

terms.definition: In-guest volume encryption with BitLocker or DM-Crypt and keys in Key Vault, retiring September 15, 2028, after which encrypted disks won't unlock on reboot.
terms.equivalent: aws: none native (EBS encrypts outside the guest) (none)

terms.definition: Encryption of a confidential VM's OS disk with keys bound to the VM's vTPM, so the disk can be decrypted only inside that attested TEE.
terms.equivalent: aws: none (none)

terms.definition: An OS disk placed on the VM's local cache or temporary storage for fast, free reimaging; it's lost on deallocation and suits stateless scale sets.
terms.equivalent: aws: instance store root volume (partial)

terms.definition: Local, non-persistent VM storage for swap and scratch data whose contents can be lost during maintenance or redeployment.
terms.equivalent: aws: EC2 instance store (close)

terms.definition: A service that versions, replicates and shares VM image definitions and VM applications across subscriptions, tenants or publicly as a community gallery, and is required for Trusted Launch custom images.
terms.equivalent: aws: AMIs with cross-account sharing and EC2 Image Builder distribution (partial)

terms.definition: A legacy single-region custom image resource, not supported with Trusted Launch, superseded by Azure Compute Gallery image versions.
terms.equivalent: aws: single-Region AMI (partial)

terms.definition: A managed service, based on HashiCorp Packer, that builds customized images from templates and distributes them to Compute Gallery.
terms.equivalent: aws: EC2 Image Builder (close)

terms.definition: A small agent-run application that configures VMs and Arc-enabled servers after deployment, such as Custom Script, monitoring agents or domain join.
terms.equivalent: aws: Systems Manager documents and EC2 user data (partial)

terms.definition: A feature that runs scripts inside a VM through the VM agent, without network access, for troubleshooting and administration.
terms.equivalent: aws: Systems Manager Run Command (close)

terms.definition: A service that assesses and installs OS updates on Azure VMs and Arc-enabled servers on demand or through scheduled maintenance configurations.
terms.equivalent: aws: Systems Manager Patch Manager (close)

terms.definition: A schedule resource that controls when guest patching or platform maintenance for dedicated hosts and isolated VMs is applied.
terms.equivalent: aws: Systems Manager maintenance window (close)

terms.definition: An IMDS endpoint that notifies a VM of upcoming reboot, redeploy, freeze or Spot preempt events so it can drain or checkpoint first.
terms.equivalent: aws: EC2 instance metadata Spot interruption notice and scheduled events (close)

terms.definition: A VM priced from unused capacity that Azure can evict with deallocate or delete policies, with up to 30 seconds' notice and no SLA.
terms.equivalent: aws: EC2 Spot Instance (close)

terms.definition: A pay-as-you-go hold on VM capacity of a size in a region or zone, backed by an SLA and without term commitment, which reservations or savings plans can discount.
terms.equivalent: aws: EC2 On-Demand Capacity Reservation (close)

terms.definition: A physical server allocated to one subscription, organized in host groups by zone and fault domain, for hardware isolation, maintenance control and licensing scenarios.
terms.equivalent: aws: EC2 Dedicated Hosts (close)

terms.definition: A service that projects servers, Kubernetes clusters and SQL Server running outside Azure into ARM via the Connected Machine agent, so tags, RBAC, Policy, Defender and Azure management services apply to them.
terms.equivalent: aws: Systems Manager hybrid managed nodes plus EKS Hybrid Nodes (partial)

terms.definition: Microsoft's Arc-enabled hyperconverged infrastructure on validated customer-owned hardware that runs VMs, AKS and AVD on-premises or at the edge, and underpins Sovereign Private Cloud.
terms.equivalent: aws: AWS Outposts (partial; Outposts is AWS-owned hardware)

terms.definition: A platform job scheduler that provisions pools of VM nodes, including Spot nodes, and runs large numbers of parallel or MPI tasks without cluster software to manage.

pairs.difference: With IaaS you still patch and secure the OS and runtime; with PaaS the provider does, so you trade control for less operational and security toil.
CapEx buys assets up front and depreciates them; OpEx pays for consumption as you go, which shifts risk of idle capacity to the provider.
Scalability is the capacity to grow by adding resources; elasticity is doing so automatically in both directions as demand changes, which is what makes consumption billing pay off.
Vertical scaling makes one instance bigger and hits a size ceiling and usually a restart; horizontal scaling adds instances and needs a distributable, mostly stateless design.

HA accepts a brief interruption during failover to meet an uptime target; fault tolerance aims for zero interruption through active redundancy, and disaster recovery restores service after a regional loss.
Residency is about where data is stored and processed; sovereignty is about whose laws and control apply, which a local region alone doesn't guarantee.

Zones protect against datacenter failure within one region at synchronous-replication distances; region pairs are a cross-region association for update sequencing and some geo-replication, and many new regions have zones but no pair.
A zonal resource is pinned to the zone you pick and fails with it unless you deploy copies; a zone-redundant resource is replicated across zones by the platform automatically.
An Azure nonzonal resource carries no zone-resiliency guarantee, whereas many AWS regional services such as S3 and DynamoDB are multi-AZ by design, so 'regional' means different things on each cloud.

A reservation commits to a specific SKU family and region for the largest discount; a savings plan commits to hourly spend, flexible across sizes and regions except EC2 Instance Savings Plans, which stay bound to a family and Region.
A reservation is a billing discount with no capacity guarantee (except AWS zonal RIs); a capacity reservation guarantees capacity with an SLA at pay-as-you-go price, and the two can be combined.

Azure RBAC authorizes ARM resource operations at management group to resource scopes; Entra roles authorize directory and Microsoft 365 administration, and a Global Administrator has no Azure access until access is elevated.
RBAC decides who may perform an action; Policy decides whether the resulting resource configuration is allowed or compliant, regardless of who requests it.

Locks are customer-applied CanNotDelete or ReadOnly controls on control-plane writes for everyone; deny assignments are created only by Azure features such as deployment stacks and can exclude specific principals or actions.
The application object is the single global definition in the home tenant; a service principal is its per-tenant instance that actually receives consent and role assignments.
System-assigned shares the resource's lifecycle and can't be shared; user-assigned is a standalone resource that can be pre-authorized, reused across resources and given federated credentials.
Managed identities serve code running on Azure resources; federation lets code running elsewhere exchange its own platform token for an Entra token, so neither needs stored secrets.

A standard FIC must match issuer, subject and audience exactly (20 per identity); a flexible FIC (preview) matches claims with wildcard expressions, so one credential can cover many branches or workflows.
Delegated permissions act on behalf of a signed-in user and are capped by that user's rights; application permissions act as the app itself and always need admin consent.
Members are internal accounts with default directory read rights; guests authenticate at their home IdP and get restricted defaults in your tenant.
Security groups grant access to resources and apps; Microsoft 365 groups also create a shared mailbox, calendar and SharePoint site for collaboration.
An eligible assignment grants nothing until activated with MFA, justification or approval for a limited time; an active assignment is in force continuously and should be the exception.

Security defaults are a free, non-customizable baseline; Conditional Access (P1) builds targeted policies with exclusions, device and risk conditions and report-only testing, and enabling it requires turning security defaults off.

Mandatory MFA is platform-enforced for Azure management sign-ins in the public cloud and can't be opted out of; security defaults are a tenant-wide setting you can disable in favor of Conditional Access.
PHS lets the cloud authenticate users with a synced hash and survives on-premises outages; PTA and AD FS keep authentication on-premises, adding infrastructure and an on-premises dependency.

Connect Sync is a full on-premises sync server managed locally; Cloud Sync uses lightweight agents configured from the cloud and is Microsoft's stated future, though some advanced scenarios still need Connect Sync.
B2B collaboration creates a guest object in your tenant; B2B direct connect creates no guest and only enables Teams shared channels under a mutual cross-tenant trust.
B2B brings partners into your employee directory as guests for your apps and Microsoft 365; an external tenant is a separate directory for your app's consumers and customers with branded sign-up.
External tenants are Microsoft's current CIAM platform built on Entra; Azure AD B2C is the legacy service with Identity Experience Framework policies and no new sales since May 1, 2025.

Application proxy publishes individual on-premises web apps with pre-authentication; Private Access gives per-app ZTNA to any TCP/UDP private resource through the Global Secure Access client, and both use the same connectors.

A private endpoint gives one specific resource a private IP reachable from peered and on-premises networks with exfiltration protection; a service endpoint keeps the public IP, only identifies the source subnet and doesn't work from on-premises.

Basic endpoints are free and authorized per subnet in each service firewall; standard endpoints are paid and tag traffic with a network identifier that a network security perimeter authorizes at scale.
A private endpoint is the consumer-side NIC that connects to a service; a Private Link service is the provider side that publishes your own service behind an internal load balancer.

NSGs are free distributed L3/L4 filters on subnets and NICs; Azure Firewall is a central, routed, stateful firewall with FQDN rules, threat intelligence and Premium TLS inspection and IDPS, and the two are used together.
Standard filters by IP, port, FQDN and threat intelligence; Premium adds TLS inspection, signature-based IDPS and URL and web-category filtering for regulated or high-risk traffic.
Detection logs matches without blocking, which is used to tune exclusions; prevention blocks matching requests and should follow a tuning period.
IP Protection is billed per protected public IP with core mitigation; Network Protection is a plan covering VNets that adds DDoS rapid response, cost protection and WAF discounts.

Load Balancer is an L4 pass-through for any TCP/UDP protocol; Application Gateway is an L7 reverse proxy in your subnet that understands paths, hosts, cookies and TLS, can host WAF and also offers a TCP/TLS proxy.

A public load balancer exposes a public frontend IP and can provide outbound SNAT; an internal one has a private frontend for intra-VNet or hybrid traffic and its backends need a separate egress method.

Front Door proxies every request at the edge with caching, TLS termination, WAF and near-instant failover; Traffic Manager only answers DNS, so clients connect directly and failover is bounded by DNS TTL.

Peering-based hub-and-spoke is customer-built and non-transitive, so spoke-to-spoke needs an NVA or firewall and UDRs; Virtual WAN Standard hubs are Microsoft-managed routers with transitive routing but less routing control.
Basic supports only site-to-site VPN; Standard adds ExpressRoute, point-to-site, inter-hub and VNet-to-VNet transit, secured hubs and routing intent.
Policy-based VPNs match traffic selectors with IKEv1 and one tunnel (Basic SKU only on Azure); route-based VPNs use routing tables and support IKEv2, BGP, P2S and active-active.
VPN Gateway encrypts traffic over the internet with variable latency and cheap setup; ExpressRoute is a private circuit with predictable latency and higher bandwidth that isn't encrypted by default.
Private peering reaches your VNets on private addresses; Microsoft peering reaches Microsoft 365 and Azure public endpoints on public prefixes selected by route filters.

NAT Gateway is an explicit, owned, scalable egress IP set you can allowlist; default outbound access is an implicit Microsoft-owned IP that can change, and new VNets now default to private subnets without it.
A private DNS zone holds records visible to linked VNets; the Private Resolver is the forwarding engine that lets on-premises query those zones and lets Azure forward to on-premises DNS.
NSG flow logs are per-NSG and retiring September 30, 2027; VNet flow logs work at VNet, subnet or NIC scope and also record AVNM admin rule decisions and encryption state.
An availability set spreads VMs across racks in one datacenter (99.95% SLA); zones spread them across separate datacenters (99.99% SLA), and the two can't be combined for the same VM.
Fault domains separate VMs across shared power and switch hardware against unplanned failure; update domains batch VMs so planned maintenance reboots only one group at a time.

Flexible manages standard VMs with mixed sizes and Spot/on-demand and full VM API support (recommended); Uniform manages identical scale-set-specific instances and remains for workloads such as Service Fabric.
Trusted Launch protects the boot chain with Secure Boot and vTPM; a confidential VM also encrypts memory in a hardware TEE so even the host and hypervisor can't read it.
Encryption at host encrypts caches, temp disks and data in flight on the host without guest CPU; ADE encrypts inside the guest with BitLocker or DM-Crypt and retires September 15, 2028.
Backup keeps point-in-time copies for restore after deletion, corruption or ransomware; Site Recovery continuously replicates running VMs to fail over a whole workload to another zone or region.

Arc is a management plane that projects existing non-Azure resources into ARM; Azure Local is hyperconverged hardware and software you buy to run Azure services on-premises, itself managed through Arc.
AVD runs session hosts in your subscription with pooled multi-session and consumption pricing; Windows 365 is a per-user fixed-price Cloud PC that Microsoft manages.

Both are the unit of billing, quota and isolation, but a subscription authenticates against an Entra tenant shared with other subscriptions, while each AWS account has its own IAM namespace and root user.
Both nest subscriptions or accounts and inherit governance, but management groups carry both RBAC grants and Azure Policy, whereas OUs carry SCPs and RCPs that only restrict and never grant.

pairs.b: AWS SCPs, RCPs, declarative policies and Config rules
pairs.difference: Azure Policy combines preventive deny, detective audit and auto-remediation on resource properties in one engine; AWS splits these across permission guardrails, Config detection and Config remediation or CloudFormation Hooks.
Both map logical zone names to physical zones differently per subscription or account; AWS exposes stable AZ IDs, while Azure exposes logical-to-physical mappings through the locations API.
Azure subnets are regional and span all zones, so zone placement is per resource; AWS subnets are bound to one AZ, so multi-AZ designs need a subnet per AZ.
Both are non-transitive private links, but Azure peering supports gateway transit to share a hub's VPN or ExpressRoute gateway, which VPC peering doesn't.
A Standard virtual hub behaves like a managed regional Transit Gateway that also hosts VPN, ExpressRoute and firewall; Cloud WAN adds a policy-defined global network with segments across Regions.

pairs.b: AWS security group and network ACL
pairs.difference: An NSG is stateful with prioritized allow and deny rules on a subnet or NIC; an AWS security group is stateful and allow-only on an ENI, while a NACL is stateless with ordered rules on a subnet.

An Azure private endpoint targets one resource; AWS distinguishes interface endpoints (a service), resource endpoints (one RDS database, instance, IP or domain via resource gateways) and service-network endpoints (VPC Lattice).

Both are managed stateful firewalls in the routed path, but Azure Firewall bundles DNAT, FQDN application rules and Premium TLS inspection, while Network Firewall uses Suricata-compatible stateful rule groups and needs a separate egress NAT gateway.

Front Door combines CDN, global L7 load balancing with origin health failover and WAF in one product; CloudFront is primarily a CDN, with origin failover groups and Global Accelerator covering the rest.
Both scale a fleet from a model with health repair; VMSS Flexible also manages zone and fault-domain spread and VM-level APIs, while ASGs rely on launch templates across AZ-bound subnets.
An availability set spreads VMs across fault and update domains for an SLA; EC2 spread and partition placement groups spread instances across racks but carry no separate SLA or update-domain concept.

Both give compute short-lived credentials from a local endpoint, but a managed identity is an Entra service principal authorized via RBAC on target resources, while an IAM role is assumed via STS with permissions in attached policies.

Both are private circuits with BGP, but one ExpressRoute circuit reaches Microsoft 365 via Microsoft peering and all regions in a geopolitical area (globally with Premium), while Direct Connect reaches Regions through Direct Connect gateways.

Entra Domain Services is a managed domain synced one way from Entra ID with no trusts to manage; AWS Managed Microsoft AD is a standalone AWS-managed forest with delegated OU administration that you can trust with on-premises AD.
Bastion brokers RDP and SSH over private IPs through a managed host in your VNet; Session Manager uses an agent with IAM-authorized sessions and no inbound ports or bastion host at all.
Agent ID makes agents first-class directory identities governed by Entra policies; AgentCore Identity manages agent workload identities and outbound credential access for agents running on AgentCore.
